notes.meaning: Balaam realizes that the Lord is fully committed to blessing Israel. He gives up his usual pagan rituals and signs because he knows they cannot change God's mind. Instead, he simply looks out toward the desert where God's people are camped.

Balaam looks down from the mountain and sees the tribes of Israel resting in neat, orderly ranks. At that moment, the Spirit of God comes upon him to give him a true message. God uses Balaam to speak His words, even though Balaam's own heart does not belong to the Lord.

Balaam begins his speech with a formal declaration of who he is. He describes himself as a man whose eyes have been opened by God to see what is hidden from others. He speaks with confidence because he knows this message comes from a higher power.

Balaam claims that he hears the very words of God and receives visions from the Almighty. The divine power causes him to fall flat on the ground in humble awe. Even while bowed low, his inner spiritual sight remains clear and sharp.

Balaam cries out in deep admiration at the sight of the camp of Israel. The thousands of tents spread out across the plains look orderly and beautiful. Their peaceful arrangement shows how well God protects and cares for His people.

The camp is compared to lush valleys, blooming gardens by a river, and majestic trees planted by the Lord. In a dry desert land, water brings rich life, growth, and coolness. These word pictures show that Israel will flourish under God's constant care.

Israel is pictured as a man carrying overflowing buckets, showing that the people will enjoy abundant water and many children. The prophecy announces that Israel's future king will be far greater than Agag, the powerful ruler of Amalek. The nation will grow into a glorious and exalted kingdom.

God brought His people out of slavery in Egypt with fierce, unstoppable strength like that of a wild ox. Because the Lord fights for them, Israel will devour their enemies and break their power. No hostile army can defeat a nation guarded by the Almighty.

Israel is compared to a resting lion that is so fierce and confident that no one dares to wake it. Balaam repeats God's ancient promise to Abraham that whoever blesses Israel will receive a blessing, and whoever curses Israel will be cursed. Balak's hope to bring a curse on them is completely doomed.

King Balak loses his temper and claps his hands together in disgust and fury. He complains bitterly that he hired Balaam to curse his enemies, but Balaam has now blessed them three times in a row. Balak realizes that his entire plan has fallen apart.

Balak furiously orders Balaam to run away and go straight back home. He sarcastically tells Balaam that the Lord has cheated him out of the royal treasures and high honors he had planned to give him. The king blames God for keeping Balaam from getting rich.

Balaam answers Balak by defending his actions. He reminds the king of the very first message he sent back with Moab's messengers. He makes it clear that he never promised to do anything on his own terms.

Balaam repeats that even a palace filled with silver and gold could not tempt him to disobey the Lord. He has no freedom to speak his own good or bad ideas. He can only say the exact words that God commands him to say.

Before leaving for home, Balaam offers one final warning to Balak. He wants to reveal what Israel will do to the people of Moab in future generations. The harm Balak wished upon Israel will end up falling on his own nation instead.

Balaam begins this last prophecy using the same grand titles for himself as before. He calls himself the son of Beor, a man whose eyes God has opened. He uses these formal words to make sure Balak takes the coming prophecy seriously.

Balaam describes himself as one who receives knowledge directly from the Most High God. He sees visions given by the Almighty, bowing low while his spiritual vision remains fully awake. This confirms that the coming message is not human guesswork, but divine truth.

Balaam looks far into the future and sees a glorious ruler coming from Israel, described as a bright star and a royal scepter. This king will strike Moab and bring down all its proud warriors. This prophecy points historically to King David, and ultimately to the Messiah, Jesus Christ.

The prophecy extends to Israel's southern neighbor, Edom, also known as Seir. Even though Edom has long hated Israel, it will be defeated and taken over as Israel acts with great courage. This was fulfilled when David placed garrisons throughout Edom.

A mighty ruler from the family of Jacob will take full command over the land. He will hunt down and defeat the enemy survivors who try to hide in fortified cities. No fortress will be strong enough to withstand his authority.

Balaam looks toward the land of Amalek and delivers a short, sharp prophecy about its future. Amalek was the first nation to attack Israel on their journey out of Egypt, but its glory will not last. In the end, Amalek will be wiped out and vanish forever.

Balaam turns his attention to the Kenites, who lived in the rugged mountain areas. Their homes sat high in the rocky cliffs like birds nesting safely above danger. Their natural defenses made them look almost impossible to conquer.

Despite their strong mountain shelters, the Kenites will slowly be worn down by hardship and war. Eventually, the mighty empire of Assyria will invade and carry them away into exile. Even the strongest natural fortresses cannot keep out God's judgment.

Balaam cries out in grief as he sees the terrible disasters that lie ahead for the nations. The coming wars and conquests will be so fierce that hardly anyone will survive. Only those whom God chooses to preserve will live through such dark times.

Warships will sail across the sea from the coasts of Cyprus and the Mediterranean to attack both Assyria and the lands beyond the river. Great empires like Greece and Rome would later crush the old powers of the East. Yet even those mighty conquerors will eventually fall into ruin and fade away.

With all the prophecies finished, Balaam and Balak separate and go their own ways. Balaam sets out in the direction of his homeland, and the king returns to his court. Balak's scheme to destroy Israel completely fails, leaving God's people safe and blessed.
